extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, aesthetics, and classical philosophy; poets and artists interested in Aristotelian poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Aristotle's and the commentator's criteria for what counts as fine art (poetry, music, dance, painting, sculpture) — especially the notion of 'imitation' (mimesis), rhythm, the universal/ideal, and the relative expressive capacities of different arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm as chief vehicle of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The dominant element in Greek music was the rhythm; 'the spirit and meaning of any given composition was felt to reside especially here' and poetry, music, and dancing constitute a group whose common element is imitation by means of rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhythm admits of application to words, sounds, and movements of the body; it has a special affinity with the nature of the soul and corresponds to symmetry in the plastic arts. The commentary links rhythm to melody and metre as primary expressive resources, and notes that rhythmical form and movement are central to poetic and musical expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's ethical/moral quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody even apart from words has an ethical quality (i.e. music can suggest or produce ἦθος).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle and his school classify melodies into ethical or affective types (ἡθικά, ἐνθουσιαστικά, πρακτικά) corresponding to the objects of imitative art (character, passion, action). The text treats sound as having a direct capacity to suggest moral qualities in a way other senses do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound as the most direct carrier of moral qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound alone carries with it any immediate suggestion of moral qualities; sight, taste, and smell are expressly excluded from this immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is qualified as perhaps an exaggeration of Aristotle; sight and colour do reflect moral character 'in however slight a degree' and often act as 'signs of moral qualities' rather than direct imitations. The passage situates hearing as pre-eminent but not absolutely exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial expression and gesture as natural, non-conventional signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Facial expression, gestures, and attitudes are a dialect which nature herself has taught and convey meaning by immediate suggestion; they are living signs, not conventional symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These natural signs enable painting and sculpture (and performance) to read and represent character without a skilled interpreter; they provide a direct link between outward form and inner movement of soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting and sculpture chiefly render outward/physical features and use signs for moral content
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting and sculpture directly render little more than the outward and physical features of an object and convey moral and spiritual facts almost wholly by signs or symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because plastic arts work through inert material and fix a frozen moment, they cannot reproduce the life of the soul in all its variety; they seize a single typical moment representative of what precedes or follows, and rely on symmetry (analogous to rhythm) and familiar signs to suggest inner qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody and metre are 'seasoning', not the essence of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody and metre (ἡδύσματα) are subordinate 'seasoning' of poetic language; the essence of poetry is imitation, not metrical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although metre and musical elements enhance charm and pleasurable emotion, Aristotle treats them as non-essential; tragedy may fulfil its function without them, though it would lack full charm. The text cites uncertainty about whether Aristotle completely denies non-metrical works the title 'poetry'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry employs symbols but not purely conventional ones; words as natural medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry produces its effect through symbol alone (except metre), employing words to call up images; yet the signs (words) used are the natural and familiar medium by which thought and feeling are revealed, not arbitrary conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry's symbols vary with race and country and require interpretation, but the representation is not 'purely symbolical' because language in life is the natural vehicle of thought and emotion; thus poetic representation still achieves likeness to human action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's subject-matter: human action and character; drama as perfect form
rubrics_metrics.description: The original which poetry reflects is human action and character in their diverse modes; in the drama the poetic imitation of life attains its perfect form, where speech corresponds to speech and action to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic imitation makes the idea of imitation in its most obvious sense apparent; poetic imitation in drama can be performed so that the play's action imitates real action directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine art imitates the universal/ideal rather than mere particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art in its highest form is an expression of the universal element in human life; it eliminates what is transient and particular and reveals the permanent and essential features (the εἶδος) of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art discovers the form towards which an object tends and produces a βέλτιον (a 'better' or ideal) which surpasses the actual. The artist's imitation is thus creative: he stamps given material with the impress of the universal form and presents a purified image of nature's original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as a creative act producing according to a true idea
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'imitate' in Aristotle's sense is equivalent to 'producing' or 'creating according to a true idea' — seizing the universal and reproducing it in simple and sensuous form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process is not mere selection/combination/embellishment; the elements must be harmonised into an ideal unity of type. The artist completes or rivals nature by realising an ideal that nature only imperfectly manifests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist must harmonise elements into an ideal unity (not mere collage)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough for the artist to select, combine, and embellish; the elements must be harmonised into an ideal unity of type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The creative work consists in stamping the given material with the impress of the universal form; harmony and unity are required so that the work expresses the 'true idea' rather than being a disconnected assemblage of beautiful parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dance equals tragedy in expressive capacity and must be perspicuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancing imitates character, emotion, and action and is 'not inferior to tragedy itself in expressive capacity'; the dancer must be perspicuous—'he must be understood though he is dumb and heard though he says nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dancer needs genius, critical judgement of poetry, memory, and mastery of mythology and gesture; dance harmonises the spectator's soul and can train moral sympathies and quiet passions. Avoid 'terrible solecisme' of ignorant performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture is not 'imitative' and thus not classed as fine art (in Greek view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture was reckoned among the useful arts by the Greeks because it lacked the 'imitative' quality regarded as essential to fine art; the decorative (sculptural) element alone is imitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a building may realise the idea of the beautiful by form and proportion, it does not in Greek notions present human life or character and therefore does not rank as fine art; the temple's metopes are a frame into which imitative sculpture may be fitted, but the building itself is 'useful'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music based on harmony treats the voice instrumentally, reducing dramatic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency of music based upon harmony is to treat the voice as one of a number of instruments, and accordingly to curtail the use of it as the great source of dramatic and emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient multiplicity of scales and changes of genus and 'colour' gave a closer reproduction of speech tones; modern harmony can make music an independent creation that no longer seeks the aid of language or reaches its aim through channels by which language influences the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine art completes nature but differs from useful art by not serving practical needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful art co-operates with nature to realise ends and serve practical needs; fine art sets practical needs aside and, by mere imagery, reveals the ideal form at which nature aims in human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist ignores intervening natural steps and presents a purified, completed ideal. Fine art is thus a completion of nature in a sense not applicable to useful art: it embodies the ideal without concern for practical modification of the real world.
